lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 7, what does a front elevation show? (A building's front, drawn flat and to scale.) Today: designing everyday objects, where form and function meet.
Function is what an object does; form is its shape and look. In 1896 the architect Louis Sullivan (1856-1924) wrote that form ever follows function: the job should shape the design.
Worked example: George Carwardine's balanced-arm lamp of 1932 uses springs, like muscles, to hold its arm still in any position. Its form, with joints and springs, comes from its function.

The Bauhaus, a school in Germany from 1919 to 1933, designed simple, useful objects for factories to make. Marcel Breuer (1902-1981) bent steel tubes into a chair in 1925, inspired by bicycle handlebars.
Ergonomics fits objects to people: a handle the right size for a hand, a seat at the right height, buttons a thumb can reach. Designers measure many people to get it right.
Phones changed form as their function changed: from a heavy desk telephone with a dial to a pocket touch screen. In 1954 Sori Yanagi (1915-2011) bent two pieces of plywood into his Butterfly Stool.
Good design today also asks: can it be repaired, made from fewer materials, and recycled? Can everyone use it, whatever their age or their hands?
Try it in the world: pick up 3 tools at home and ask how each handle fits a hand. In LIFE, open the Tool Book to see tools designed for their jobs. Next: animation.

exercises.hint: Function and job mean nearly the same.
exercises.explain: Function is what an object does; its shape and colour are its form.

exercises.hint: Start at the bottom, where it stands, and go up to the light.
exercises.explain: The heavy base stands on the desk; the arm reaches up, the springs hold it, and the shade points the light.

exercises.prompt: Form follows function means the job should shape the design.
exercises.hint: Which comes first: the job or the look?
exercises.explain: True: work out the job first, then give it a form that does the job well.

exercises.prompt: Match each object to its function.
exercises.hint: Ask what job each one does.
exercises.explain: A lamp lights, a chair holds someone sitting, a phone carries voices and a stool is a backless seat.

exercises.prompt: Which part do you turn with a finger to make a call?
exercises.hint: Look for the wheel with holes.
exercises.explain: You put a finger in a hole of the dial and turn it to send each number.

exercises.prompt: How it works, or how it looks?
items: a heavy base stops it tipping
exercises.hint: Would the lamp still work without it?
exercises.explain: Springs, joints and a heavy base make it work; a glossy finish and a pattern are about its look.

exercises.prompt: Put these phones in time order.
items: a mobile phone the size of a brick
a desk telephone with a dial
exercises.hint: Think of how phones got smaller and gained screens.
exercises.explain: Dials came first, then push buttons (the 1960s), then brick-sized mobiles (the 1980s), then touch screens (from 2007).

exercises.hint: Sit on it in your mind: what holds you up, and what does your back rest on?
exercises.explain: You rest your back on the backrest and sit on the seat; the legs stand on the floor and the frame joins them.

exercises.prompt: Marcel Breuer's steel chair of 1925 was inspired by a bicycle's handlebars.
exercises.explain: True: the bent steel tubes of handlebars gave him the idea.

exercises.prompt: A handle is too wide for a child's hand. Which design idea is this about?
exercises.hint: Which idea fits objects to people's bodies?
exercises.explain: Ergonomics is fitting objects to the people who use them, such as the size of a hand.

exercises.prompt: A chair's seat is 45 cm high, and its back rises 40 cm above the seat. How high is the top of the back?

exercises.hint: Look at the top, the side and the bottom edge.
exercises.explain: The screen fills the front; the camera is at the top; the button is on the side; the speaker and microphone are on the bottom edge.

exercises.prompt: Why did Bauhaus designers keep shapes simple?
choices: so factories could make them for everyone
exercises.hint: Who made the objects, and for whom?
exercises.explain: Simple shapes could be made well and cheaply in factories, so good design reached everyone.

exercises.prompt: Easy to repair, or hard to repair?
exercises.hint: Could you open it and fix one part?
exercises.explain: Screws, spare parts and a guide make repair easy; glue and a sealed battery make it hard.

exercises.prompt: Designing for everyone means thinking of people who are older, younger, or use one hand.
exercises.hint: Who might find an object hard to use?
exercises.explain: True: good design works for as many people as possible.

exercises.prompt: The balanced-arm lamp's springs work most like which part of a body?
exercises.hint: What in your arm holds it still in the air?
exercises.explain: Muscles pull to hold an arm still; the springs pull to hold the lamp's arm still.

exercises.prompt: A stool is drawn at 1:5. The drawing's seat is 9 cm high. How high is the real seat, in cm?
exercises.hint: At 1:5 everything real is 5 times the drawing.
